text: Heads, I riffle shuffle a sorted deck four times. Tails, a computer shuffles it perfectly. From the deck alone, how often could you tell which? Pick 50, 75, or 100%. Monte Carlo samplers move by random steps, like these riffles. Stop them too early, and they still remember where they started. The obvious check is the top card, the one you'd be dealt. Here's how often each card ends up there after four riffles. Almost flat. Only the old top card stands out, one time in 15. Judging by the top card, you'd be right 52% of the time. Four riffles look like plenty. A guesser who sees the whole deck does far better. The model cuts near the middle, then drops cards from each half in proportion to its size. Each half stays in order, so one riffle leaves two rising sequences. Runs of consecutive cards, reading left to right. Give each sequence its own level. The cut crosses each level once, so a riffle can at most split it in two. Three riffles. Eight. Four riffles. At most 16, this deck has 14. A perfect shuffle averages 26 and a half and gives 16 or fewer once in 2 million decks. Call 16 or fewer Riffled and you'd be wrong about once in 4 million games. The top card can't see this. It lives in the order between cards. Bayer and Diaconis proved that in this model, decks with the same count are equally likely. So pile decks onto their counts. every possible deck weighted by its chance The red area purple above blue is the distance from random Right now it one how many more riffles to bring it below a half a fifth riffle 0 a sixth point six one a seventh point three three guess riffled where purple is higher you catch 65 percent of riffled decks and flag 32 percent of perfect ones accuracy is a half plus half the difference, and the difference is the red area. Each riffle roughly halved the gap, but blue's spread, its standard deviation, stayed about 2. While the gap spans several spreads, the distance stays near 1. Within about one spread, it halves every riffle, that's the cliff. Multiply each gap by 2 to the K, and it settles near 230. divide that by two each riffle, and it reaches one spread after just under seven. For n cards, 230 grows like n squared, but the spread only like root n, so the cliff sits near three halves log base two of n. Aldus proved that law. Bayer and Diaconis computed the exact curve. For 52 cards, seven riffles is the first count below a half. Trefethen and Trefethen measured information instead. No cliff, and five or six shuffles do a reasonable job. Many Markov chains share this cliff, and samplers share the trap. One statistic can settle, like the top card, long before the whole chain has. Back to the coin flip. After four riffles, you'd almost never be wrong, same as with an unshuffled deck. three more riffles, and you'd be right only two times out of three.
